extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, HR professionals, worker advocates, and other stakeholders affected by or commenting on FLSA EAP exemption rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic standards used by the Department of Labor to set and update the executive/administrative/professional (EAP) exemption salary and HCE compensation thresholds, estimate affected workers, and comply with information-collection requirements under the PRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-test structure for EAP exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1940, the regulations implementing the exemption have generally required each of the following three tests to be met: (1) the employee must be paid a predetermined and fixed salary that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of work performed (the salary basis test); (2) the amount of salary paid must meet a minimum specified amount (the salary level test); and (3) the employee's job duties must primarily involve executive, administrative, or professional duties as defined by the regulations (the duties test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule continues to rely on these tests; salary and duties together determine exemption status for most salaried white-collar employees. The salary test serves as an easily applied index of the bona fide character of employment and can save parties from applying a time-consuming duties analysis to large groups who will not pass it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary basis test
rubrics_metrics.description: The employee must be paid a predetermined and fixed salary that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of work performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remains a required component of the EAP exemption determination as described in part 541; applies in conjunction with the salary level and duties tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary level test (final methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is adjusting the standard salary level by setting it equal to the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region (currently the South), based on the most recent year of CPS data at the time of drafting (using BLS 2023 data produces $1,128 per week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice is intended to restore overtime protections for salaried white-collar employees who historically were nonexempt under the long test while still allowing employers to use the exemption for many lower-paid white-collar employees who were exempt under prior standard duties tests. The methodology contrasts with prior rules (e.g., 20th percentile in 2019, low-end-of-short-test in 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly Compensated Employee (HCE) total compensation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCE total annual compensation requirement is adjusted to the annualized weekly earnings of the 85th percentile of full-time salaried workers nationally ($151,164 using 2023 data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selected percentile is intended to keep the HCE test high enough to exclude all but those at the very top of the economic ladder and to preserve the HCE test's intended function as a minimal-duties, high-compensation exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triennial updating mechanism for earnings thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will update the standard salary level and HCE total compensation requirement initially on July 1, 2024 and every 3 years thereafter to reflect current earnings data, in accordance with the methodology used to set each threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updating is based on whatever methodology is in place at the time of the update; if new methodologies are invalidated, the updating provision would use the prior methodologies (e.g., 2019 methods) as the baseline. The provision is intended to ensure thresholds reflect current earnings and to provide certainty and stability for employers and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of rule provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is including a severability section, §541.5, to make clear that all the rule's provisions are separate and severable and should be given the fullest possible effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is drafted so provisions can function independently and includes discussion of how various provisions can operate sensibly if another provision is stayed, enjoined, or declared invalid. This is consistent with ACUS guidance and is not an acknowledgment of legal vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) compliance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PRA, an agency may not collect or sponsor an information collection requirement unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. Agencies must consider the need for their information collections, the collections' practical utility, the impact of paperwork burdens on the public, and how to minimize those burdens, and must solicit public comment on proposed changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department solicited public comment on proposed burden changes to ICRs (OMB control numbers cited) and will submit ICRs to OMB upon publication of the final rule. The rule does not impose new information collection requirements but may increase burdens under existing requirements due to a larger universe of covered employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB control number display and ICR handling
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB has assigned control number 1235-0021 to the complaint information collection and 1235-0018 to Records to be kept by Employers—FLSA; during rulemaking a duplicate ICR was created (initially 1235-0NEW, later assigned 1235-0035) to allow public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department must address comments received during the NPRM comment period and resubmit for approval at time of final rule; OMB notices guided the Department's resubmission process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information collection scope and effect (PRA analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: This rulemaking revises 29 CFR part 541 and affects collections including (1) the complaint process for potential violations of laws WHD enforces and (2) disclosure and recordkeeping requirements for covered employers under the FLSA. The rule does not add new ICRs but increases burdens because the pool of workers for whom employers must maintain records grows, and more employees may file complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRA section includes regulatory familiarization costs (duplicative with economic analysis) and summarizes estimated respondent/respondent burden and costs for the affected ICRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping form flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no particular order or form of records prescribed by the regulations; a respondent may meet the requirements using paper or electronic means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This flexibility is noted when considering employer burden and system adjustments; actual recordkeeping requirements are not changing, but the number of workers requiring records will increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint intake process to reduce burden
rubrics_metrics.description: WHD uses a complaint filing process in which complainants discuss concerns with WHD professional staff; this process allows agency staff to refer complainants raising concerns that are not actionable under federal wage and hour laws to another agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process reduces burden caused by filing complaints that are not actionable and is part of PRA burden-minimization considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CPS MORG data and pooling methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: All estimates of numbers of workers used in this analysis were based on CPS MORG data. To increase sample size the Department pooled 3 years of CPS MORG data (2021–2023). Earnings for 2021 and 2022 were inflated to 2023 dollars using CPI-U and observation weights were adjusted so pooled sample represents the 2023 total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pooling yields roughly three times as many observations to represent the same total number of workers in 2023, improving characterization of subsets (occupation, industry, geography). This pooled dataset is used to estimate all impacts of the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of respondents with varying weekly hours and missing hours detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department eliminated workers who reported that their weekly hours vary and who provided no additional information on hours worked because it cannot estimate effects for these workers (unknown overtime exposure), and reweighted the rest of the sample to keep the same total employment estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adjustment assumes the distribution of hours worked by workers whose hours do not vary is representative of hours worked by workers whose hours vary — the Department considers this appropriate absent more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population exclusions for affected-worker estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis excludes workers who are unemployed, not subject to its regulations, or not covered by the FLSA (e.g., military on active duty, unpaid volunteers, self-employed without earnings data, many Federal employees regulated by OPM, most religious workers); some covered Federal workers (USPS, TVA, Library of Congress) are included. The FLSA does not cover employees of firms with annual revenue less than $500,000 not engaged in interstate commerce, but the Department did not exclude them due to lack of data. The Department also excluded blue-collar workers, hourly-paid workers, and workers exempt under certain other (non-EAP) exemptions (including certain agricultural and transportation workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department followed methods from prior rulemakings and GAO guidance; exclusions were implemented via occupation, industry, and other CPS variables. Appendix A in docket contains detailed criteria for some exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation approach for affected EAP workers
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate the number of workers affected by the rule, the new standard salary level and the new HCE total annual compensation threshold are applied to the earnings of current EAP-exempt workers, because no data source identifies workers as EAP exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is consistent with 2004, 2016, and 2019 final rules. After sequential exclusions, the Department estimated 53.5 million salaried white-collar workers who might be claimed as EAP exempt and are the population for which the thresholds are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for selecting percentile-based methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department explains choices of percentiles for thresholds (35th percentile for standard salary in lowest-wage Census Region; 85th percentile nationally for HCE) to balance restoring protections for historically nonexempt salaried workers and allowing employers to use the exemption for many lower-paid white-collar employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percentile choices are compared to historical approaches (long test, short test, single-test) and prior rules (2004, 2016, 2019) to justify anticipated distributional and coverage effects; the Department discusses tradeoffs in exemption scope and administrative practicability.
